questions.question: The user taps the button three times. What does the text show?
options: Count: 0 every time, since a plain var is not observable state
Count: 3, because Compose tracks changes to all local variables
It crashes: a local var can't be changed from inside onClick
Count: 1, then it resets to 0 on the next tap of the button
questions.explanation: Compose only recomposes when snapshot state it read changes; a plain local `var` is not tracked, so nothing is redrawn. Even if something else caused a recomposition, the function would run again and reset `count` to 0. Use `var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`.

questions.question: A value held with `remember { }` survives recomposition but is lost on a configuration change such as rotation, while `rememberSaveable { }` survives it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `remember` stores the value in the composition, which is rebuilt when the Activity is recreated. `rememberSaveable` also writes the value to the saved instance state, so it is restored after rotation and even after process death, as long as the type can be saved.

questions.question: `vm.name` emits a new value. Which composables run again?
options: Screen and Greeting run; Header is skipped
Only Greeting, because Screen never needs to run again after setup
Screen, Header and Greeting all run again on every new name value
The whole tree under setContent is re-executed from its root
questions.explanation: `name` is read in Screen's body, so Screen's restart scope is invalidated and re-executes; `Column` is inline, so it is part of that same scope. Greeting gets a new argument and recomposes, while Header takes no parameters and is skipped. Compose recomposes the smallest scopes that read the changed state, not the whole tree.

questions.question: Which of these are safe to do directly in a composable function's body? Select all that apply.
options: Read state and compute values to display
Call `analytics.log("screen_shown")`
Emit other composables such as Text and Row
Start a network call with `scope.launch { }`
Write to a `MutableState` that it also reads
questions.explanation: Composable functions can run many times, in any order, and recomposition can be skipped or cancelled, so the body must be free of side effects. Logging or launching work there fires on every recomposition, and writing state you read causes an endless recomposition loop. Put such work in `LaunchedEffect`, `SideEffect` or event callbacks.

questions.question: This crashes with an error saying the value cannot be saved using the current SaveableStateRegistry. Why?
options: Filters can't go into a Bundle; make it @Parcelize Parcelable or pass a Saver
rememberSaveable only accepts primitive values such as Int, String and Boolean, nothing else
mutableStateOf can't be used inside rememberSaveable; it must return the raw Filters value
Data classes need a no-argument constructor before rememberSaveable can recreate them
questions.explanation: `rememberSaveable` writes into a Bundle, so the value must be a type a Bundle can hold: primitives, String, Parcelable, Serializable and so on. Wrapping a saveable value in `mutableStateOf` is supported. For a plain class, add `@Parcelize` or give it a `Saver` such as `mapSaver` or `listSaver`.

questions.question: Which of these cause a composable that reads the value to recompose? Select all that apply.
options: A `MutableState` it reads is set to a different value
A StateFlow it collects with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` emits a new value
A plain `var` property on the ViewModel is reassigned
An item is added to a `mutableStateListOf()` it iterates
An item is added to an `ArrayList` stored in `mutableStateOf`
questions.explanation: Recomposition is driven by snapshot state: `MutableState`, snapshot collections like `mutableStateListOf`, and flows converted to State. A plain property is invisible to Compose. Mutating an `ArrayList` in place does not change the `MutableState`'s value, so no read is invalidated.

questions.question: Why wrap this in `remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }` instead of computing it directly?
options: Without it, every index change recomposes; derivedStateOf fires only when the Boolean flips
derivedStateOf runs the computation on a background thread so scrolling the list stays smooth
Read directly, the value is computed once and never updates while the user scrolls the list
derivedStateOf keeps the computed value across configuration changes, unlike direct reads
questions.explanation: Reading `firstVisibleItemIndex` in composition subscribes the composable to every change of the index, so it recomposes constantly while scrolling. `derivedStateOf` reads the index itself and only invalidates readers when its result changes, here when it goes between false and true. It runs on the same thread and saves nothing across recreation.

questions.question: With strong skipping (the default since the Kotlin 2.0.20 Compose compiler), the parent recomposes and passes a new `List<Item>` instance with equal contents. Does `ItemList` skip?
options: No: unstable parameters are compared by instance (===), and this is a new instance
Yes: strong skipping compares every parameter with equals(), and the lists are equal
No: a composable that has unstable parameters can never be skipped by the runtime
Yes: under strong skipping a child always skips when only its parent recomposed
questions.explanation: Strong skipping makes composables with unstable parameters skippable, but compares those parameters by identity; only stable parameters are compared with `equals`. `Item` has a `var`, so it and `List<Item>` are unstable, and a new list instance means ItemList recomposes. Keeping the same instance (or making the types stable, e.g. an immutable collection of stable classes) lets it skip.

questions.question: Under strong skipping, lambdas passed to composables are automatically remembered, even when they capture unstable values.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With strong skipping, the compiler wraps lambdas in composable functions in a `remember` keyed on their captured values, comparing unstable captures by instance. So a recomposition no longer creates a new lambda that breaks skipping of the child, as long as the captures are the same instances. Before strong skipping, only lambdas capturing stable values were memoized.

questions.question: The screen is reused when `userId` changes from "a" to "b". What does `formatter` hold afterwards?
options: The formatter built for "a", because remember has no key and keeps its first value
A new formatter for "b", since remember reruns when any parameter of the function changes
A new formatter for "b", but only once the composable leaves and re-enters composition
It throws, because remember can't capture a parameter of the enclosing composable
questions.explanation: `remember { }` without keys computes once per position in the composition and returns the cached value afterwards, so it keeps the stale formatter. Pass the inputs as keys, `remember(userId) { createFormatter(userId) }`, to recompute when they change. Parameters of the enclosing function are not implicit keys.
